body_markdown:
## Introduction


A greenfield Nutanix Government Cloud Clusters (GC2) deployment with no internet or on-premises connectivity is straightforward because its management plane stays inside the customer’s VPC. Migrations work differently and cannot use that isolated design. Nutanix Move needs a working path between its appliance, the source environment and the GC2 target before it can transfer a VM. This article explains why that path matters, who owns it, and what to line up before you schedule a migration so you can submit a complete connectivity request the first time.


In a Department of Defense design, the path from AWS to the Internet or back to on-premises traverses the Secure Cloud Computing Architecture (SCCA) Virtual Data Center Security Stack (VDSS). This article treats the VDSS as a separately managed transit VPC and security boundary. The exact implementation varies by organization, so the team responsible for the VDSS must confirm the real end-to-end path and policy.


When supporting GC2 deployments in GovCloud for DoD mission owners, the critical theme is planning and preparation. Early connectivity testing between the source and target replication appliances is essential, as it surfaces network or policy obstacles before they can derail the migration timeline. Teams should also build adequate lead time into the migration schedule to accommodate their command’s procedure for processing an Exception to Policy (E2P) if one is required, since securing that approval can add weeks to the effort.


Two factors work in the migration’s favor, because the traffic remains on the Non-classified Internet Protocol (IP) Router Network (NIPR-to-NIPR), the connectivity path is straightforward, and because the migration itself is a temporary activity, it faces fewer hurdles than a permanent architectural change would. That said, no two mission owners or their VDSS policies are exactly alike, and those differences can disrupt even the most careful planning and execution. Confirm the VDSS path and begin the E2P process early, and the cutover becomes a scheduling exercise rather than a blocker.


GC2 supports migrations with Nutanix Move. Nutanix Move is an included migration tool that transfers VMs into Nutanix AHV, NC2 or GC2 from ESXi, Hyper-V, AWS EC2 or Azure VM with minimal downtime. Move orchestrates guest preparation, driver injection and incremental data seeding, so the workload keeps running until a short cutover window at the end. For large environments, multiple appliances can be used to scale and accommodate a greater number of migration activities.


Each migrated VM uses native AWS networking and receives a native AWS IP address. VPN, Direct Connect and Transit Gateway can provide on-premises connectivity when the customer’s approved design calls for them. GC2 target networking is direct. The hard prerequisite is the approved route through the VDSS.


## **Add a Network to the Nutanix Cluster**


Native networking on GC2 is a two-step process, and there’s no Nutanix overlay to reconcile afterward.


1. Create the AWS subnet in the GC2 VPC (gc2-subnet.yaml CFT, or the approved subnet-creation path for your account) and associate it with the route table you want the workloads to use.
2. Add it as a subnet on the cluster from Prism Element. On the current GC2 build you have to do this in Prism Element, not Prism Central: subnet creation from Prism Central isn’t supported on pc.7.3.1.12 in US-Gov-West, US-Gov-East or the EU Sovereign region.


From there each VM gets a native AWS IP from that subnet, so AWS routing applies to the VM exactly as it would to an EC2 instance: VPC route tables, security groups, Transit Gateway, VPN and Direct Connect, plus reachability to S3, RDS and the rest of the account’s services with no gateway VM, no NAT hop and no tunnel into the cluster. The networking work moves back to where the AWS team already does it, and the Nutanix side is just “which subnet does this vNIC land in.”


## Map the complete path


Document the traffic path in both directions before deploying Move:


` On-premises AHV or ESXi source -> on-premises routing and firewall -> VPN or Direct Connect -> SCCA VDSS transit VPC and firewall -> Transit Gateway, if used -> GC2 VPC -> Move appliance and GC2 target`


Record every source and destination CIDR on that path. GC2 VPC, cluster, UVM, on-premises and transit ranges must not overlap. While it’s out of the scope of this article, Nutanix can provide stretch layer 2 with Flow Virtual Networking, even with using native subnets.


## Size the pipe


A reachable path is not the same as a usable one. Reachability decides whether the migration starts. Packet size and throughput decide whether it finishes inside the maintenance window.


### Packet size and fragmentation


Move’s data path to the CVMs is NFS on TCP/UDP 2049, so it sends large writes with the don’t-fragment bit set. That makes MTU the first thing to settle:


**Path element** **MTU behavior**


AWS Site-to-Site VPN 1446 bytes, MSS 1406, no jumbo frames, and no Path MTU Discovery


Transit Gateway, VPC, Direct Connect, peering and Connect attachments 8500 bytes


Transit Gateway, VPN attachments 1500 bytes


Transit Gateway clamps the maximum segment size on all packets, and it performs Path MTU Discovery only for traffic entering on VPC and Connect attachments. It does not do so on VPN, Direct Connect or peering attachments, and a VPN connection doesn’t support discovery at all.


Clamp MSS at the on-premises edge rather than relying on discovery. A VDSS firewall that drops ICMP fragmentation-needed messages turns an MTU mismatch into a black hole, and a black hole presents as a migration that hangs rather than one that fails with an error.


## What MSS clamping actually does


Two hosts opening a TCP connection each advertise a maximum segment size in the SYN packet, and that value is derived from the MTU of the interface they’re sending from. A source host on a 1500-byte LAN advertises an MSS of 1460, which is 1500 minus 20 bytes of IPv4 header and 20 bytes of TCP header. Neither host knows that the path narrows to 1446 bytes inside the VPN.


MSS clamping is a router or firewall rewriting that advertised value as the SYN passes through. Set the clamp to 1406 for an AWS Site-to-Site VPN and both hosts negotiate segments that fit the tunnel, so nothing on the path ever needs to fragment. The alternative, Path MTU Discovery, depends on an ICMP fragmentation-needed message getting back to the sender, and that message crosses the VDSS in the opposite direction to the traffic that triggered it. Firewalls filter it routinely, and AWS Site-to-Site VPN doesn’t support discovery in the first place.


Two limits on clamping:


1. It applies to TCP only, because there is no MSS option in UDP, so the UDP portmapper and NFS traffic on 111 and 2049 still depends on a correctly sized MTU end to end.
2. It only takes effect on connections whose SYN crosses the device doing the clamping, so a device added mid-path after sessions are established changes nothing until those sessions restart. Transit Gateway clamps on its own for traffic it carries, but that covers only the AWS portion of the path, not the hop between the source environment and the VDSS.


## Throughput ceilings


Size the transfer against the slowest hop, not the fastest:


**Path element** **Ceiling**


Standard VPN tunnel 1.25 Gbps, 140,000 packets per second


Large bandwidth VPN tunnel 5 Gbps, 400,000 packets per second


Transit Gateway Connect peer 5 Gbps, 300,000 packets per second


Transit Gateway VPC, Direct Connect and peering attachments Up to 100 Gbps and 7,500,000 packets per second per Availability Zone


Table 1: Networking Throughput


The tunnel is almost always the constraint. Equal-cost multipath spreads separate flows across tunnels, so it raises aggregate throughput but not the rate of any single transfer, and it requires dynamic routing. A statically routed VPN gets no aggregation.


Packets per second deserves its own look. On a tunnel already carrying production traffic, the packet rate can run out before the bit rate does.


Where the data volume makes the arithmetic uncomfortable, Direct Connect changes the shape of the problem rather than tuning it: dedicated bandwidth, an 8500-byte MTU through Transit Gateway, and no tunnel packet ceiling.


## What Move controls, and what it doesn’t


Nutanix Move limits concurrent disk migrations to protect the source environment, so transfer parallelism isn’t an open dial. It does support bandwidth throttling policies per source provider, with schedules in recent versions, which is the right way to keep seeding out of the production window. Use the performance matrix for large data migration in the Move documentation for sizing rather than estimating from link speed alone, and plan the cutover close behind the seed, because change accumulates against it while the seed is in flight.


**Note:**
Two failure modes that aren’t about capacity but appear during long transfers: a stateful firewall can time out a long-lived NFS session mid-seed, which looks like a stall rather than a block, and a VDSS performing deep inspection applies its own throughput ceiling well below the link’s rated speed. Ask for the inspected throughput number to size the migration plan.


Fig 1. GC2 architecture with Nutanix Move


Use the following order for the build and test.


**1. Deploy GC2 and confirm its network objects**


Deploy the GC2 VPC, subnets and cluster with the approved CloudFormation templates. In an account where the deployer isn’t permitted to create, pass or assume IAM roles, have an administrator precreate the roles first with the optional GC2 1.2 IAM templates. The companion articles cover that path:[GC2 1.2’s New IAM Improvements: Old Way vs. New Way](https://www.dwaynelessner.com/articles/gc2-iam-old-way-vs-new-way/) for the reasoning, and[Deploying GC2 with Precreated IAM Roles: The Four-Step Sequence](https://dwaynelessner.com/articles/gc2-iam-deploy-steps/) for the order. Confirm that the UVM subnet intended for Move has enough addresses and a route table associated with the required path. GC2 uses private IPv4 CIDRs for cloud-associated subnets.


Record these values in the as-built:


- GC2 VPC and UVM subnet CIDRs
- Move appliance IP address
- Cluster virtual IP address and target CVM addresses
- On-premises AHV CVM addresses or ESXi host and vCenter addresses
- Transit Gateway attachment and route-table IDs, when used
- VDSS ingress and egress interfaces
- AWS network ACLs and security groups attached to the UVM subnet and Move appliance


GC2 creates three security groups during deployment. These will be used to allow traffic into the GC2 cluster.


**GC2 security group** **Purpose** **Migration action**


<cluster-stack>-InternalManagement-<id> AHV-to-CVM traffic Do not edit


<cluster-stack>-ClusterSecurityGroup-<id> UVM-to-CVM management traffic, CVM to CVM traffic if using Nutanix DR. Verify target-side Move ports


<cluster-stack>-AllUVMSecurityGroup-<id> Traffic entering or leaving all UVMs Place approved workload-access rules here


Table 2: GC2 Security Group Edits in AWS


**2. Establish the routed SCCA path**


A tunnel or Direct Connect virtual interface can report healthy while carrying no migration traffic. Each routing domain must know both the source and return prefixes.


Check the path as separate hops:


1. The on-premises router sends the GC2 UVM and cluster prefixes toward the approved VPN or Direct Connect connection.
2. The AWS-side VPN or Direct Connect configuration carries routes for the on-premises source, administration and guest-network prefixes plus the GC2 prefixes.
3. The VDSS transit route tables send GC2-bound traffic toward the GC2 attachment and return traffic toward the on-premises attachment.
4. If Transit Gateway is present, its route-table association and propagation place both sets of prefixes in the correct table. Add static routes where the design doesn’t use propagation.
5. The route table associated with the GC2 UVM subnet sends on-premises prefixes toward the approved transit target.
6. Every return route follows the same approved security path. An alternate return path can break a stateful firewall session even when the forward route is correct.


The VDSS firewall is a separate control. Submit a rule request with named source CIDRs, destination CIDRs, ports, protocols and direction. Approval in the VDSS does not change an AWS security group, and an AWS security-group rule does not pass the VDSS boundary. If this VDSS firewall request requires an Exception to Policy, that E2P approval is the long-lead item the introduction flagged—submit the request as early as the path design allows, not when you’re ready to migrate.


**3. Deploy and register Move**


Deploy the Nutanix Move appliance in the selected GC2 UVM subnet after the routed path exists. Confirm that the appliance receives an address from that subnet and uses the expected route table, network ACL and UVM security group.


From an administration workstation, connect to Move over TCP 443. Register the on-premises source and the GC2 target with the correct management addresses. If registration uses hostnames, verify DNS resolution from the Move appliance as part of the path test.


Do not start with a migration plan and use its failure as a network diagnostic. Source and target registration should succeed first.


**4. Edit or verify the AWS security-group rules**


Make workload-access changes in` <cluster-stack>-AllUVMSecurityGroup-<id>` . Do not add broad rules to` <cluster-stack>-InternalManagement-<id>` .


For Nutanix Move, apply these checks:


1. Identify the Move appliance’s UVM subnet and confirm which GC2 UVM security group its interface uses.
2. Add a narrowly scoped inbound TCP 443 rule from the administration CIDR.
3. Add inbound TCP 443 from source guest-network CIDRs only when guest preparation requires guest-to-Move HTTPS. AHV or NC2 guests can use this path for preparation. ESXi guests need it only for manual preparation.
4. Never use` 0.0.0.0/0` . Use approved on-premises, VDSS or administration CIDRs.
5. Verify outbound connectivity from Move to the source environment and target CVMs. The default UVM group defaults to permit all outbound traffic.


Target CVM access uses` <cluster-stack>-ClusterSecurityGroup-<id>` . This security group will have TCP/UDP 111 and 2049 plus 9440 in the default User Management rules. Verify the deployed rules.


The live Nutanix Move Ports and Protocols page can be found[here](https://portal.nutanix.com/page/documents/ports-and-protocols?productType=Move) . For an on-premises AHV or ESXi source and a GC2 target, keep the rule review to these flows:


**Source** **Destination** **Service** **Ports**


User workstation Nutanix Move HTTPS TCP 443


Nutanix Move AHV or NC2 source CVMs Prism and NFS TCP 9440; TCP/UDP 111 and 2049


Nutanix Move AHV, NC2 or ESXi-on-Nutanix target CVMs Prism and NFS TCP 9440; TCP/UDP 111 and 2049


Nutanix Move ESXi source hosts NFC TCP 443 and 902


Nutanix Move vCenter HTTPS TCP 443


AHV/NC2 source guest Nutanix Move Guest preparation HTTPS TCP 443


ESXi source guest Nutanix Move Manual preparation HTTPS only TCP 443


Table 3: Needed edits for the Cluster Security Group


These rows describe endpoint requirements. The VDSS firewall and each network ACL still need policy that permits the same path.


**5. Validate each hop**


Test from the endpoint that will originate each connection. A successful administration login to Nutanix Move proves only the workstation-to-Move path.


Build an evidence table for the change record:


**Test** **Expected result** **Evidence**


Administration workstation to Move, TCP 443 Move UI responds Client test and Move access log


Move to source AHV CVMs, TCP 9440 and TCP/UDP 111, 2049 Source registration and data path succeed Move validation and source logs


Move to source ESXi hosts, TCP 443 and 902 NFC path succeeds Move validation, ESXi logs and firewall logs


Move to vCenter, TCP 443 vCenter registration succeeds Move validation and vCenter events


Move to target CVMs, TCP 9440 and TCP/UDP 111, 2049 Target registration and data path succeed Move validation and target logs


Source guest to Move, TCP 443, when required Guest preparation reaches Move Guest test and Move log


Table 4: Testing the Network path


For every failed row, inspect the route tables, Transit Gateway association and propagation, network ACL, AWS security group and VDSS policy. VPC Flow Logs can show whether traffic reached an AWS interface. VDSS firewall logs can show whether the separate security boundary accepted or denied it. One log source cannot account for the entire path.


Check the return route explicitly after any one-way timeout. A forward route plus a missing return route often looks like a port block.


**6. Migrate a pilot VM**


Choose one nonproduction VM that represents the source hypervisor and guest-preparation method planned for the larger migration. Run Nutanix Move’s checks before transfer, then monitor the pilot across the VDSS path.


**Note** : Supported Guest Operating Systems for[Nutanix Move](https://portal.nutanix.com/page/documents/details?targetId=Nutanix-Move-v6_3:top-supported-os-azure-r.html) .


After cutover, confirm the VM’s native AWS IP address, default gateway, DNS resolution and application dependencies. Test access from the approved administration and workload networks. The original Source VM will be shut down, so there is always an easy way to fail back if needed.
